query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys (HEAs) for high-temperature applications, increasing the relative concentration of slow-diffusing, high oxygen-affinity elements (Al and Cr) will promote selective oxidation that forms and retains a dense, adherent protective oxide scale (primarily Al2O3 and/or Cr2O3), thereby reducing overall oxidation kinetics compared to alloys with lower Al/Cr content.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic HEA such as CoCrFeNiMn (baseline) exhibiting a homogeneous single-phase structure.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition to increase the atomic percentages of Al and Cr by a controlled amount (e.g. substituting a portion of Mn with Al and Cr) while keeping processing conditions equivalent.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation tests conducted in air at high temperatures (e.g. 900 °C) for a fixed duration (e.g. 24 hours) under identical oxygen partial pressures.
generation.structural_mediator: A layered oxide scale wherein an inner, dense, protective Al2O3/Cr2O3 layer forms preferentially due to the slower diffusion kinetics of Al and Cr, while any non-protective oxides (potentially forming from Mn) are minimized.
generation.mechanism: Differential diffusion kinetics govern the oxidation behavior: Al and Cr have lower diffusion rates and higher oxygen affinity, leading to their preferential oxidation and formation of a compact, adherent barrier that retards further oxygen ingress. In contrast, fast-diffusing elements like Mn, which tend to form non-protective, porous oxides, are reduced in concentration, thus shifting the oxide formation towards a protective regime.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline HEA (equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn), the modified alloy (with enhanced Al/Cr content) will exhibit significantly lower oxidation weight gain (e.g. an expected reduction on the order of 30–50% under similar high-temperature conditions) and form a microstructure displaying a uniform, adherent protective oxide layer.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn HEA exhibiting layered oxide scales with a significant presence of non-protective Mn-rich oxides, leading to higher oxidation kinetics.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate in high-temperature oxidizing environments (approximately 800–1100 °C) and may depend on oxygen partial pressures. At temperatures too low, diffusion is insufficient, and at excessively high temperatures, volatile oxide species (e.g. CrO3) might form, altering the protective behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative impact on oxidation kinetics will depend on the precise compositional changes, processing history, and testing conditions. There is also uncertainty regarding the optimum Al/Cr ratio that maximizes protective scale formation without compromising alloy stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set being the baseline equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn and the other with a controlled increase in Al and Cr content (e.g. replacing a fraction of Mn with Al and Cr). Subject both sets to identical isothermal oxidation tests at 900 °C in air for 24 hours.
measurements: Thermogravimetric analysis to record oxidation weight gain
Cross-sectional TEM/SEM with EDS mapping to characterize the oxide scale structure and composition
X-ray diffraction (in situ or ex situ) to identify oxide phases present
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g. less than ~10% difference) in oxidation weight gain or fails to form a uniform, dense protective oxide scale compared to the baseline, then the hypothesized mechanism attributing protection to enhanced selective oxidation by Al and Cr is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, CrMnFeCoNi HEA behaviour responding to changes in temperature and environmental factors such as the partial pressure of oxygen has been investigated by in situ XRD at high temperatures up to 1100 °C. In situ thermal observations of materials with the high-temperature XRD provide unique information such as temperature-dependent phase transformations, types of new phase formation, and the start and finish temperatures of competing phases in an alloy system []. In situ HTXRD is instrumental in revealing the real-time of oxide formation as well as the type and temperature at which various kinds of oxide form when metals are exposed to high temperatures in air or in another simulated environment. Our HTXRD analysis provided insight into the thermal stability, phase transitions, and high-temperature oxidation behaviour of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy samples, which provides significant guidance in the development of high-performance alloys for demanding applications. The surface and cross-sectional microstructure, elemental distributions, and oxide compositions have been examined to further understand the evolution of the oxides. In alloys for high-temperature applications, at least one protective oxide among BeO, Cr2O3, Al2O3, and SiO2 are desirable to form, and that is why most of the alloys for high-temperature applications add these elements to form an oxide barrier for better oxidation resistance []. Previous studies have indicated that Cr2O3 is the sole stable phase in the Cr-O system, known for its compact structure and superior oxidation resistance []. However, it is noteworthy that Cr2O3 was not detected in the in situ XRD analysis conducted for this study. It can be reasonably inferred that non-existence of a Cr2O3 layer caused further outward diffusion of Mn, leading to the formation of Mn3O4, as can be seen from the XRD scan at a temperature of 950 °C.

Cr’s outward diffusion is faster than oxygen’s inward diffusion, so chromia scales usually grow outward, consisting of fractions of iron, nickel, and manganese. However, at temperatures above 900 °C, chromia can form volatile CrO3. Aluminum, another effective alloying element, forms a protective Al2O3 layer, offering significant resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion. Al2O3 scales grow slower than chromium oxide scales and are more stable, especially against aggressive carbon or sulfur species. However, the formation of alumina and consequent depletion of Al in the alloy could result in structural instability in the alloy. The formation of oxide scales in HEAs containing multiple oxide-forming species is influenced by their intricate chemistries and microstructures. High-temperature, long-duration oxidation studies on bulk alloys typically reveal dominant oxide films composed of complex ternary and quaternary oxides. The polycrystalline nature of these alloys, combined with surface heterogeneity and phase instabilities at high temperatures, leads to highly variable oxide structures. A coarse grain microstructure having BCC/B2 phases was obtained in the as-cast HEA sample. Only 5 min of straining of sample significantly refined the grain structure from 98 to 1 μm and 0.43 μm for the SFP_400 and SFP_1800 sample, respectively. The ultrafine-grained samples showed a phase transition from BCC/B2 to FCC structure. The SFP_400 sample showed a 12–20% reduction in the oxidation kinetics, whereas the SFP_1800 sample showed a 38–48% reduction in the oxidation kinetics compared to the as-cast alloy. Low values of parabolic rate constant and high values of activation energy for the ultrafine-grained samples show the high oxidation resistance of the processed samples. Protective oxide scales of Al2O3 and Cr2O3 were predominantly found after discontinuous isothermal oxidation. Other than protective scales, the availability of Co(Cr,Fe)2O4 spinel phases was also observed during the oxidation at elevated temperatures. The presence of more GBs favoring outward flux of elements to form a dense chromia layer followed by internal Al-rich oxide layered structure is responsible for the enhanced oxidation resistance of the processed samples.

cited_evidence.text: The high-temperature oxidation at 800 °C was evaluated based on the weight gains of the initially weighted sample with a defined surface. As one can see in Figure 14, the Mn15Al5 alloy showed a sort of parabolic kinetics of oxidation, which is known for rapid weight gain in a matter of minutes and slowing down over time due to the diffusion-driven character of oxygen transport through the developing oxide layer. However, as the annealing prolonged, the oxidation kinetics showed rather a linear mechanism according to the weight gains, suggesting the poor protective behavior of such layer due to, e.g., cracking or formation of pores within the layer. On the other hand, increasing the Al content resulted in logarithmic kinetics of oxidation, suggesting the creation of a dense protective layer, which did not tend to chip off over the time of annealing. Both the Mn10Al10 and Mn5Al15 alloys gained less than 5 g m−2 of newly formed oxides after 100 h annealing at 800 °C. Similar behavior was also reported in the work of Lyu et al. papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Ex situ and in situ TEM observations at 400 °C with controlled oxidation to reveal layered oxide structures
papers.findings: A 20 nm oxide layer develops with a compositional sequence: a Ni-rich pre-oxide layer, followed by a Cr2O3-rich inner layer and an outer oxide containing Fe, Mn, and Co. Rapid formation of compositional layers was evident even after 2 minutes of oxidation.
papers.mechanism: Differential diffusion rates and sequential oxidation of alloying species lead to a layered oxide structure; slower-forming species (Cr) establish a barrier while more mobile species (Mn) later form non‐protective oxides.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Insights into the Oxidation Mechanisms of CrMnFeCoNi High-Entropy Alloy Using In Situ X-ray Diffraction.
papers.approach: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) experiments in different environments (air and vacuum) combined with thermodynamic (CALPHAD) modeling
papers.findings: In air, vigorous oxidation produced primarily spinel-type oxides with significant Mn depletion; in vacuum, only MnO (halite-type) was observed. Notably, protective oxides such as Cr2O3 were not detected, which contrasts with some earlier studies.
papers.mechanism: The oxidation behavior is governed by the fast outward diffusion of Mn, leading to formation of non-protective oxide layers; the balance of cation diffusivities and oxygen incorporation appears central to whether a continuous protective layer forms.

papers.title: An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide.
papers.approach: Long-term isothermal oxidation tests at 1000 °C and 1100 °C monitored by thermogravimetric analysis and microstructural characterization
papers.findings: At 1100 °C, superior oxidation resistance was observed with a parabolic mass gain profile attributed to the formation of a dense, external CrTaO4-based oxide layer. Reduced Ti content in NV1 was linked to this selective oxidation behavior.
papers.mechanism: Selective oxidation results in the nucleation and growth of a CrTaO4-based layer that impedes outward diffusion of oxidizable species and oxygen ingress, thus acting as a protective barrier.

papers.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Comparison of as-cast coarse-grained and ultrafine-grained samples via controlled oxidation tests at elevated temperatures
papers.findings: Ultrafine-grained samples exhibit markedly reduced oxidation kinetics (38–48% reduction) relative to coarse-grained alloys, along with the formation of predominantly protective Al2O3 and Cr2O3 scales.
papers.mechanism: Increased grain boundary density in ultrafine-grained alloys enhances the rapid nucleation and formation of dense, adherent protective oxide layers.

papers.title: Influence of the Al Content on the Properties of Mechanically Alloyed CoCrFeNiMnXAl20-X High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: Al-containing CoCrFeNiMn-based HEAs with varying Al and Mn contents
papers.approach: High-temperature oxidation tests at 800 °C comparing different alloy compositions with variable Al and Mn ratios
papers.findings: Increasing Al content led to logarithmic oxidation kinetics and formation of dense, protective oxide layers, while Mn-rich compositions exhibited rapid, parabolic oxidation and non-protective oxide growth.
papers.mechanism: The relative diffusivities and oxygen affinities of Al versus Mn control oxide layer quality; higher Al favors formation of protective Al2O3, whereas high Mn promotes rapid, non-protective oxide formation due to its high mobility.

established: Protective oxide layers (e.g., Al2O3, Cr2O3, CrTaO4) enhance oxidation resistance in HEAs at high temperatures.
Differential diffusion rates of alloying elements (such as Mn, Cr, and Al) govern the composition and structure of the oxide scale.
A dense, adherent oxide barrier can significantly slow further oxidation and weight gain under high-temperature exposure.

approaches_tried.approach: In situ HTXRD coupled with thermodynamic modeling to track phase evolution during oxidation
approaches_tried.outcome: Provided real-time insights into phase formation and revealed that expected protective oxides sometimes do not form (e.g., absence of Cr2O3 in CrMnFeCoNi HEA); highlighted the role of Mn depletion.

approaches_tried.approach: Long-term isothermal oxidation tests on refractory HEAs
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated the protective effect of a CrTaO4-based oxide layer on oxidation resistance at 1100 °C; linked alloy composition adjustments (reduced Ti) to improved performance.

approaches_tried.approach: Grain refinement via mechanical processing (e.g., surface deformation) to increase grain boundary density
approaches_tried.outcome: Resulted in enhanced oxidation resistance due to rapid and uniform formation of protective oxide scales.

mechanisms: Differential diffusion kinetics of alloying elements where slower-diffusing species (Al, Cr) form dense protective oxides while faster-diffusing species (Mn) lead to less protective, porous oxide growth.
Selective oxidation that favors the nucleation and growth of protective oxides (e.g., CrTaO4 or Al2O3) which act as barriers to further oxygen ingress.
Enhanced oxide layer formation at grain boundaries in refined microstructures that promotes uniform, adherent protective scales.
disagreements: Some studies report the formation of Cr2O3 as a dominant protective layer, while others (e.g., in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA investigation) did not detect Cr2O3, suggesting variations in oxidation behavior dependent on testing conditions and alloy composition.

The role of Mn is contentious; while its high mobility can cause rapid oxidation and depletion leading to non-protective oxides, its presence is also inherent in certain HEA formulations, challenging the straightforward assignment of its role in protection.
open_questions: What is the precise balance in diffusion kinetics among multiple alloying elements (e.g., Al, Cr, Mn) that determines when a protective oxide layer forms?
How do subtle changes in composition and microstructure (such as grain size) quantitatively influence the nucleation and growth of protective versus non-protective oxides?
What are the long-term stability limits of various protective oxide layers (e.g., CrTaO4, Al2O3) in extended high-temperature exposure regimes?
opportunities: Conduct controlled comparative studies by systematically varying key element ratios (especially Al, Cr, and Mn) in HEAs and monitoring oxide scale formation in situ across a range of temperatures and oxygen partial pressures.
Utilize combined microstructural (e.g., TEM, SEM-EDS) and in situ diffraction techniques to correlate grain boundary density and diffusion pathways with the emergence of protective oxide phases.

Investigate the influence of long-term oxidation (beyond 48 hours) to identify threshold conditions at which protective layers degrade, providing a direct testable parameter to falsify mechanistic predictions regarding oxide layer stability.

directions.direction: Modify the alloy composition to enhance the content of slow‐diffusing, high oxygen-affinity elements (e.g. Al and Cr) relative to fast-diffusing elements (e.g. Mn), thereby promoting the selective formation of a dense, adherent oxide (Al2O3/Cr2O3) that impedes further oxygen ingress.
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the mechanistic basis of selective oxidation through differential diffusion kinetics. The literature supports that elements like Al and Cr form protective oxides (see PMC11169556::web::003::introduction and PMC9692591::web::022::3_3_thermal_stability_and_high_temperatu). The physics of oxidation and cation diffusion in complex alloys are well established; moreover, systematic composition tuning is feasible and highly informative.

directions.direction: Refine the grain structure via mechanical processing (e.g. severe plastic deformation) to increase grain boundary density, which can accelerate uniform nucleation of protective oxide phases.
directions.assessment: While enhanced grain boundary density can provide additional oxidation nucleation sites (supported by PMC9026100::web::024::conclusion), its effect is more indirect on the diffusion kinetics of specific elements. This direction is feasible but may not isolate the influence of elemental diffusivities as clearly.

directions.direction: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment to develop an initial ultrathin protective scale, followed by high-temperature exposure to assess scale retention.
directions.assessment: Pre-oxidation treatments can establish protective layers, yet they do not elucidate the intrinsic mechanism governing oxide layer composition. While such protocols can improve overall oxidation resistance, they may mask the role of the differential elemental diffusion.

directions.direction: Employ in situ high-temperature XRD or TEM studies combined with CALPHAD modeling to simultaneously monitor phase evolution and diffusion kinetics during oxidation.
directions.assessment: This approach is powerful for mechanistic insights and real-time observation. However, it is more diagnostic than interventional and may not directly test how modifications in composition affect protective oxide retention.

directions.direction: Introduce surface modification coatings that are designed to promote selective oxidation of passivating elements in situ, and compare against uncoated counterparts.
directions.assessment: While surface coatings can significantly improve oxidation resistance, they do not directly address the intrinsic alloy mechanism of selective oxide formation and retention driven by differential diffusion kinetics.

choice.direction: Modify alloy composition to increase the relative content of slow-diffusing, high oxygen-affinity elements (Al and Cr) to promote selective formation of dense protective oxides.
choice.why: This direction most directly addresses the mechanistic hypothesis by controlling the diffusion kinetics of key alloying elements. Prior evidence indicates that protective oxides such as Al2O3 and Cr2O3 form when these elements preferentially oxidize while fast diffusing species like Mn are suppressed (see PMC11169556::web::003::introduction and PMC10384371::web::027::4_3_oxidation_in_air). The approach is supported by well-established physics and offers a clear, falsifiable prediction under controlled high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
